newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economy seen growing strongly in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economy seen growing strongly in 1996.

text.p: The Philippine economy is likely this year to post the highest growth in gross national product (GNP) since 1988 but overheating is not a worry, the government's top economic planning official said on Friday.

Cielito Habito, the secretary-general of the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) and socioeconomic planning secretary, said early indications have shown strong exports and manufacturing growth in the fourth quarter.
The economy expanded by an annualised 7.1 percent in the first three quarters of the year.
"It's very likely that we will extend the surge in the fourth quarter this year," Habito told reporters.
That would make 1996 the strongest year of growth in the Philippines since 1988, when the country posted 7.7 percent GNP growth before it was devastated by a coup and severe power outages.
Next year, the government is expecting the GNP to expand by 7.0 to 8.0 percent and gross domestic product by 7.1 percent to 7.8 percent, Habito said.
"Is our economy about to overheat? Well, my answer is an emphatic No! ... In fact, it is almost amusing for me that people start worrying about overheating," Habito added.

He said inflation has been kept in check, with the consumer price index rise slowing to a year-on-year 4.5 percent in November and a likely full-year average of less than 8.5 percent against 8.1 percent in 1995. Inflation in 1997 is pegged at 6.5 percent.
Fiscal and external balances were improving, while infrastructure projects were rapidly expanding in order to accommodate bigger turnover, Habito added.
"Our economy is still well below our full capacity ... Any references to overheating are somewhat misplaced at this point in time," he added.
"We are not going to see a boom-and-bust cycle as we have done before. I'd rather say all we are going to have is a boom-boom-boom in the years ahead."

Vaughn Montes, chief economist of Citibank NA of the Philippines, agreed saying the current growth could be sustained over the next three to four years following the series of economic reforms undertaken by the government.
"It is important to point out that the growth is based on sound macroeconomic policies. There are some important reforms that are ... driving the growth," Montes said.

However, University of the Philippines professor Joseph Lim said the widening trade deficit, which hit a record high of $10.09 billion in the first 10 months, could pose a threat to the current high economic growth and steady inflation rate regime.
He said that an overvalued peso has hurt exporters and encouraged imports.
"I think the current trade gap might explode one day and that it might lead to devaluation and with it, spiralling inflation," Lim said.
As a remedy, Lim called for a devaluation of the currency, a move which monetary authorities have ruled out.
